common_name: Kate Bletilla (Variegated Cream-Margined Hardy Ground Orchid)

planting.note: Plant pseudobulbs or divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Kate bears cream-margined variegated foliage that adds ornamental value even before the plant flowers.

directions: Plant pseudobulbs or divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, mulching to protect the shallow pseudobulbs over winter in the colder parts of its hardiness range. Kate produces attractive, pleated, lance-shaped leaves edged in crisp cream-white variegation, giving the plant garden interest well before its orchid-like magenta-pink flowers open in late spring on slender stems held above the foliage. Unlike most terrestrial orchids, which are notoriously fussy, this species is remarkably easy and reliable in an ordinary garden border with consistent moisture, spreading gradually by offset pseudobulbs into a fuller clump over the years. Established plantings need little care beyond a yearly topdressing of compost and division every several years if clumps become overcrowded.

common_name: Black Coral Snake Plant (Dark Wide-Leaved Sansevieria)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix; Black Coral bears exceptionally dark green, wide, upright leaves.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix. Black Coral bears broad, stiffly upright, exceptionally dark green leaves with faint gray-green banding, a deeper, more solid color than the typical mottled green of common snake plant, giving the plant a bold, architectural presence. Like other snake plants it is extremely tolerant of low light, infrequent watering, and general neglect, making it one of the easiest and most forgiving houseplants available, and it also tolerates outdoor container culture on a shaded porch in warm-summer climates. Water only when the soil is fully dry and avoid overpotting, which encourages root rot in this slow-growing succulent; in USDA zones below its hardiness range, bring containers indoors before the first fall frost.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

common_name: Bantel's Sensation Snake Plant (Narrow White-Striped Sansevieria)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix; Bantel's Sensation bears narrow leaves with fine, vertical white-and-green striping, a more delicate look than common snake plant cultivars.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix. Bantel's Sensation forms slender, stiffly upright leaves finely striped in white and dark green, a more delicate, refined texture than the broader, more heavily mottled foliage of common snake plant cultivars, giving it a distinctive vertical, grass-like presence. Like other snake plants it tolerates low light, infrequent watering, and general neglect exceptionally well, making it one of the most forgiving houseplants available, and older leaves may occasionally revert to plain green, which should be removed at the base to keep the clump true to type. Water only when the soil is fully dry and avoid overpotting, which encourages root rot in this slow-growing succulent.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

common_name: Golden Hahnii Snake Plant (Dwarf Gold-Margined Rosette Sansevieria)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix; Golden Hahnii is a dwarf, rosette-forming snake plant with bright gold-margined leaves, well suited to small pots and dish gardens.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix. Golden Hahnii forms a low, dense, bird's-nest-like rosette of broad, dark green leaves edged in a bright golden-yellow margin, a variegated sport of the compact Hahnii cultivar rarely more than a foot across, well suited to a small pot, dish garden, or tabletop planting. Its bright variegation holds up well in the bright indirect light it needs to grow properly, though direct hot sun can scorch the leaf margins. Like other snake plants it tolerates infrequent watering and general neglect exceptionally well, and watch for and remove any reverted all-green growth to keep the clump variegated. Water only when the soil is fully dry and avoid overpotting, which encourages root rot in this slow-growing succulent.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

common_name: Whitney Snake Plant (Dwarf Silver-Green Mottled Sansevieria)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix; Whitney is a dwarf, rosette-forming snake plant well suited to small containers, dish gardens, and windowsill growing.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix. Whitney forms a low, dense rosette of broad leaves mottled in silvery gray-green, a dwarf, compact form that stays well under a foot tall and wide, making it well suited to a small pot, dish garden, or windowsill planting where a full-size upright snake plant would be too large. Like other snake plants it is extremely tolerant of low light, infrequent watering, and general neglect, making it one of the easiest houseplants for beginners or low-light spaces. Water only when the soil is fully dry and avoid overpotting, which encourages root rot in this slow-growing succulent; it also does well in a shaded outdoor container through the warm season.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference
